questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A reported attempt to stop publication
questions.learningObjective: Identify a government attempt to restrain publication
questions.stem: Your apiary logbook notes that a county official telephoned the editor asking her to hold a story about a stolen honey crop. Which description of that request is accurate?

options.text: It is a prior restraint, because the government tried to stop publication before it occurred
It is harmless, because nobody compelled the editor to print anything
options.misconception: treats the absence of force as the absence of restraint

options.text: It is a libel problem, because the story would damage the official's reputation
options.misconception: redirects the issue to a defamation claim

options.text: It is harmless, because the editor was always free to refuse the request
options.misconception: assumes the outcome removes the constitutional problem

questions.explanation: An attempt to stop a story before it appears is a prior restraint, which is heavily suspect whether or not the editor complies. Refusing the request does not remove the attempt from scrutiny.
questions.hint: Ask whether the government tried to stop publication first.

questions.stem: Your logbook records the reach of three local rules: one bans every item of a certain kind, one bans only items of that kind that cause a specified harm, and one bans nothing but requires a licence. Which rule most clearly raises the question of a law that reaches more than its object?

options.text: The licence rule, because requiring permission always burdens expression
options.misconception: treats licensing as inherently overbroad

options.text: None of them, because local rules are never measured against their object
options.misconception: assumes local rules are exempt from review

options.text: The harm-specific rule, because naming a harm always narrows the rule
options.misconception: assumes specific wording cures overbreadth

options.text: The broad prohibition, because it may sweep in cases the harm does not require

questions.explanation: A rule is broader than its object when it reaches conduct the harm it addresses does not require. The question is how much legitimate activity the rule sweeps in.
questions.hint: Compare each rule with the harm it is meant to address.

questions.stem: Your diagram tracks voter rules in two lines: line one shows state elections and a two-year state residence requirement; line two shows national elections and a fifty-day residency rule drawn by federal statute and upheld in court. What does the diagram illustrate?

options.misconception: assumes one period fits all elections

options.misconception: misstates the split between state and federal elections

options.text: That state and national elections may carry different residence periods
That residence requirements are never valid for any election
options.misconception: treats all residency rules as invalid

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The clause on commerce among the several states
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Congress may reach purely local business activity
questions.stem: You explain to a new hive partner why the federal government can reach a family business in your county that sells only to local customers. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Congress may regulate commerce among the several states, and the Supreme Court has read that power broadly. A local seller whose goods move in interstate commerce may be reached because the activity is commerce, and later the Court held that Congress may also regulate intrastate activity that substantially affects interstate commerce, so the market is treated as an economic whole.

questions.explanation: The commerce power reaches activity that is part of the national market, so a local seller is not exempt because its customers are nearby. Congress may reach intrastate activity affecting commerce.
questions.hint: Ask how the local business connects to the national market.

questions.explanation: Subtract the required state period from the time served: three years in the state minus two leaves one more year. The country requirement is already met by the eight years recorded.
questions.hint: Subtract the state requirement from the years served.

questions.stem: On the basis of that note, which analysis of the state credit is most accurate?

options.text: The credit is valid, because the state may reward businesses that stay within its borders
options.misconception: treats local preference as a valid state policy

options.text: The credit is invalid, because no state may give any tax preference of any kind
options.misconception: reads the limit as a ban on all preferences

options.text: The credit is valid, because tax credits are a matter of state fiscal policy
options.misconception: insulates fiscal measures from scrutiny

options.text: The credit likely burdens interstate commerce and invites scrutiny under the commerce clause

questions.explanation: A state measure favouring business kept inside its borders while penalising commerce across state lines is likely invalid, and a fiscal rationale does not rescue it. The limit targets discrimination.
questions.hint: Ask whether the credit favours in-state trade.

questions.topic: Naming the clause and the standard for a display rule
questions.learningObjective: Name the clause and standard governing a government display

stimulus.body: A county council voted to hang a motto on the wall of its public meeting hall and to keep the display in place permanently. A resident asked the county to explain which constitutional clause governs the decision and what standard applies to it.

questions.stem: Taking the council note as the record, what is the best answer to the resident's question?

options.text: The first amendment requires strict scrutiny of any message displayed by a government body
options.misconception: treats government speech as ordinary private speech

options.text: The first amendment applies only if the display is paid for by private donors
options.misconception: ties the clause to the source of funding

options.text: The first amendment is the relevant clause and the government speech doctrine applies
There is no clause to name, because a public hall belongs to the council alone
options.misconception: assumes property ownership removes constitutional limits

questions.explanation: The first amendment is the clause to name. Where government speaks for itself on its own property, the government speech doctrine applies and it must not discriminate on viewpoint.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Naming what is required and from which clause
questions.learningObjective: Name a clause and state its requirement precisely
questions.stem: Your club's study group asks you to prepare a reference sheet that names a constitutional clause and states exactly what it requires, using the honey-harvest inspection case in your logbook as the example.

answer.exemplar: The relevant clause is the import and export clause, which forbids a state from laying any imposts or duties on imports or exports without the consent of Congress, except such inspection laws as are absolutely necessary to execute. So the state may inspect goods coming into the state, but it may not use the inspection power as a device for raising revenue.

questions.explanation: The clause forbids state duties on imports and exports without congressional consent while allowing necessary inspection laws. The line between an inspection fee and a revenue device marks the limit.
questions.hint: Name the clause before you describe the requirement.

It was an inquiry about facts, because no order was signed
options.misconception: treats the absence of a written order as decisive

options.misconception: reduces the attempt to editorial annoyance

options.text: It was a subpoena, because the sheriff's office was investigating a theft
options.misconception: relabels the episode as a compulsory process

questions.explanation: An attempt to prevent publication before it happens is a prior restraint whether it comes from a deputy, a sheriff or a private figure acting for the government. No signed order is needed.

options.text: It is valid, because the harm was real and the ordinance stops it
options.misconception: assumes a real harm justifies any scope

options.text: It is vulnerable, because it reaches far beyond the mischief the council described
It is valid, because advertising on property is not protected at all
options.misconception: denies protection to commercial speech outright

options.text: It is valid, because the council acted on a complaint from one resident
options.misconception: treats a complaint as the measure of legality

options.text: State B, because a fifty-day county rule exceeds the limit for national elections
options.misconception: invents a limit on county residency

options.text: State C, because a two-year state residency rule is too restrictive
None of them, because residence periods are never subject to review
options.misconception: assumes voting rules are unreviewable

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The uniform rule of naturalisation
questions.learningObjective: Explain the uniform rule and its federal requirements
questions.stem: A visiting relative asks you to explain why the federal naturalisation rule must be the same in every state, and what the rule actually requires of an applicant. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The naturalisation clause lets Congress set a uniform rule for naturalisation, which means federal standards apply the same way in every state, and Congress may not use nationality to rank applicants. The rule requires five years of residence in the country, two years in the state, continuous residence, good moral character, and a demonstration of basic English, and the applicant must apply in person.

questions.explanation: Uniformity means federal standards apply identically everywhere and cannot be tuned to favour some nationalities. The rule also sets concrete requirements of residence, character and language.
questions.hint: Explain both the uniformity and the listed requirements.

options.misconception: assumes permits avoid constitutional limits

options.misconception: assumes strict scrutiny for all sign regulation

The state constitution alone governs, because no federal clause covers signage

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A reported attempt to stop publication
questions.learningObjective: Explain why restraints are treated more strictly than punishments
questions.stem: You write a short note for the club handbook explaining why government efforts to stop publication are treated differently from government efforts to punish what was published.

answer.exemplar: A prior restraint stops speech before it reaches the public, which removes the public's chance to judge the value of the expression and to respond to it, so courts begin with a presumption against such restraints. Punishing speech after publication leaves the information circulating and can be handled through ordinary channels such as defamation law, so the restraint is the more serious interference.

questions.explanation: Stopping a story before it appears removes it from public view, while punishing what has been published leaves it in circulation. That asymmetry explains the strong presumption against restraints.
questions.hint: Ask what each remedy prevents the public from seeing.

questions.explanation: A law is vulnerable when it reaches far more protected activity than the harm it addresses, so a court asks how much lawful activity the rule removes along with the offending leafleting.
questions.hint: Ask how much lawful activity the rule removes.

questions.topic: The constitutional limit on state duties at the border
questions.learningObjective: State the rule and exception governing state border duties
questions.stem: You are asked to write, for the club's handbook, the rule that limits what a state may do to goods that cross its border, and the exception it allows.

answer.exemplar: The import and export clause forbids any state, without the consent of Congress, to lay imposts or duties on imports or exports, and the clause's own exception allows only such inspection laws as are absolutely necessary to execute the inspection power. So a state may inspect incoming shipments and charge the cost of that inspection, but it may not use the border to collect revenue.

questions.explanation: The clause is a limit on state revenue power at the border, not on inspection itself. The line is drawn at the cost of a genuinely necessary inspection, and beyond that the state is laying a duty.
questions.hint: State the rule first, then the narrow exception.

questions.topic: Naming the clause and the standard for a display rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two standards that can apply to display rules
questions.stem: You are asked to explain, for a visiting school group, how a court's approach differs depending on whether a government display rule governs private speakers or the government itself.

answer.exemplar: Where a rule governs private speakers, the first amendment applies in its usual form, so a content-based rule is measured by strict scrutiny and a content-neutral rule by whether it is narrowly tailored and leaves open ample alternatives. Where the rule concerns the government's own message on its own property, the government speech doctrine applies and the requirement is that the government not discriminate on the basis of viewpoint.

questions.explanation: The same clause governs both, but the standard differs because government speech is not private speech. Private rules are judged by neutrality and tailoring; government display by viewpoint.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking before naming the standard.

questions.topic: Different residence periods for state and national elections
questions.learningObjective: Explain the origin of the difference between election periods
questions.stem: You write the club's explainer on why voters in state elections and voters in national elections can face different residence periods.

answer.exemplar: Courts have struck down long state residency requirements for voting because they burden the right to vote, while permitting short federal periods for national elections, on the view that the fifty-day limit is adequate for voting. The result is that a person who moved recently may vote for federal candidates but not for state office, which the decisions treat as a lawful difference between the two kinds of election.

questions.explanation: The difference comes from how courts weighed long residence rules against administrative need. Federal elections keep a short period, and state rules must stay within what courts have allowed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Naming what is required and from which clause
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to name a clause and its requirement
questions.stem: You prepare the club's reference note explaining how to name a constitutional clause and state its requirement without vagueness.

answer.exemplar: Name the clause in its own terms and then state what it obliges or forbids, in language a person could check. For example, the fourth amendment requires a warrant supported by probable cause before a search unless an exception applies, and the naturalisation clause requires a uniform rule of naturalisation with the same requirements in every state. Vague phrases such as proper safeguards or fair procedure will not do, because they name nothing that can be applied.

questions.explanation: Good clause naming pairs a specific provision with a concrete requirement that can be checked against facts. Vague wording defeats it, because no one can tell whether it has been met.
questions.hint: Pair the clause with a requirement that can be checked.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The clause on commerce among the several states
questions.learningObjective: Explain the breadth of the commerce reading and its cost
questions.stem: You write the section of the club's handbook that explains why the Court reads the commerce clause broadly and what that breadth has cost businesses like the ones at the fairground.

answer.exemplar: The Court reads the commerce clause broadly because it treats the national market as an integrated whole, so a rule that ignores a state's small share of that market could break the whole system apart, which is why the power reaches activity inside a single state that has a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The cost is that a local business may be caught by a federal statute that never mentioned it, and the business must then show the effect was substantial.

questions.explanation: The breadth comes from treating the market as an integrated whole, and the price is that local actors can be reached by federal law. Businesses in the trade often press for a substantial effect.
questions.hint: Explain both the reason and the price of the reading.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A reported attempt to stop publication
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hold request is judged more strictly
questions.stem: You explain to the club why a government's request that a newspaper hold a story is treated more strictly than its prosecution of a story already printed.

answer.exemplar: A request to hold a story stops the expression before the public has seen it, which deprives the public of the chance to judge the information and to respond to it, so courts begin with a strong presumption against restraints of that kind. Prosecuting a published story leaves the information in circulation and puts the burden on the government to prove the wrong, so the two remedies are not treated alike.

questions.explanation: The timing of the remedy is what separates them, because a restraint removes expression from the public and a prosecution leaves it available. That asymmetry produces the stronger rule for restraints.
questions.hint: Ask what each remedy does to the public's access.

options.text: The second arrow, because publishing is itself the violation
options.misconception: treats publication as the offending act

options.text: The third arrow, because a written order against further publication restrains the press
The fourth arrow, because any penalty after publication is unconstitutional
options.misconception: treats all post-publication penalties as barred

questions.explanation: A written order forbidding further publication is the most serious interference, because it restrains the press on the strength of the objection. Earlier requests and later penalties differ.
questions.hint: Ask which step directly forbids publication.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A law that reaches more than its object
questions.learningObjective: Explain why good motives do not cure an overbroad rule
questions.stem: You prepare the club's essay explaining why a law that is broader than its object is treated as a problem even when the government had good reasons for the law it passed.

answer.exemplar: A law that reaches further than the harm it addresses curtails more freedom than the justification supports, and where a narrower rule would have served the same purpose the court may read the statute narrowly or strike the sweeping version. That is a rule about the fit between means and ends, so good motives do not rescue a law whose sweep exceeds its object, although a genuine interest may support a rule drawn more broadly.

questions.explanation: The doctrine asks whether the breadth of the rule is justified, so a good reason for the law is not enough. Where a narrower rule would work, the court narrows or invalidates the wider version.
questions.hint: Ask about the fit between the rule's reach and its purpose.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Different residence periods for state and national elections
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of voters affected by a residence rule
questions.stem: Your notes record that a state residence rule for voting in state office elections excludes voters who moved less than 90 days before the election. If 2,700 of the state's 45,000 registered voters fall in that group, what percentage of registered voters does the rule exclude?
questions.explanation: Divide the affected voters by the registered total and convert: 2,700 divided by 45,000 equals 0.06, or 6 percent. A rule that reaches even a small share can be challenged as a burden on voting.
questions.hint: Divide the affected voters by the registered total.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The clause on commerce among the several states
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a court weighs a state burden on interstate traffic

stimulus.body: A state law required every shipment of goods arriving by truck to be unloaded and inspected at a state facility before delivery. An out-of-state carrier challenged the law, and the court asked how the burden on interstate traffic compared with the benefit the state expected to gain.

questions.stem: From the case note, which statement best describes the court's enquiry?

options.text: It asked whether the carrier had complied with the inspection requirement
options.misconception: confuses the enquiry with a compliance question

options.text: It weighed the burden on interstate commerce against the local benefit of the rule
It asked whether the state would lose money if the law were repealed
options.misconception: treats the fiscal effect as the measure

options.text: It asked whether other states imposed similar inspection rules
options.misconception: makes the comparison with other states the test

questions.explanation: A state regulation burdening interstate commerce is judged by weighing the burden against the local benefits it produces. That is the enquiry recorded, not a question about compliance or other states.
questions.hint: Ask what the court weighed against what.
